Japan core inflation soars to highest this year as energy subsidy expiry pushes up consumer prices
body: Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy prices and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy.
Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month.

Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before.

Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher energy prices brought about by the Iran war. Japan has reportedly approved reintroduction of energy subsidies in December to stave off higher imported energy prices as higher prices crimp growth, hitting consumption and net exports.

October inflation reading is likely to push the Bank of Japan toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 75% chance of a 25 basis point hike from the Bank of Japan."The BOJ is likely to look through the temporary weakness in 3Q GDP and focus instead on underlying inflation and wage dynamics," Ma Tieying, senior economist at DBS Group Research, wrote in a Monday note.

news.title: Fed's Paulson keeps quiet on December, says October’s pause was never meant as a stop
body: With no fresh policy signal, the speech is unlikely to move rate pricing, and a quarter-point December hike remains the strong favourite. Her “pause was not a stop” framing supports the view that the hiking cycle runs into 2027, which keeps front-end Treasury yields and the dollar supported. Her three triggers for faster hikes give traders a checklist for the 4 December payrolls report and other data before the meeting: inflation expectations, wage growth and underlying inflation. An upside surprise on wages or expectations would strengthen the case for the larger move that Waller has floated.
Paulson argues the Fed should need to say less if markets understand it, and her policy view hasn’t changed: gradual hikes, with three clear reasons to go faster.

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson stayed away from any near-term guidance on interest rates on Thursday. In a speech in New York, she argued that the Fed communicates best when the public understands how it thinks, not when officials spell out what comes next. With no fresh steer ahead of the December 8 to 9 meeting, her policy views from earlier this month remain the best guide to how she is likely to vote.

Speaking to the Money Marketeers of New York University, Paulson said understanding matters more than the particular ways the Fed communicates. If markets grasp the Fed’s reaction function, she argued, officials need to say less each time new data arrive, and policy can stay steady and largely predictable. She said the value of rate-path guidance depends on circumstances and is less useful in normal times, though Fed communications should still be clear about officials’ views.

She pointed to October as an example. The Fed held rates steady after hiking in September, but markets still expected further tightening, so the pause did not leave policy behind. In her words, shared understanding allowed policy to move deliberately, “without the risk that a pause was mistaken for a stop.” That was the closest she came to a signal: the October hold was a breather, not the end of the cycle.

Her remarks fit a wider debate inside the Fed. Under Chair Kevin Warsh, the central bank has shortened its policy statement and set up a task force on communications. Warsh himself has largely stepped back from giving rate guidance, even as many other officials continue to share their views.

Paulson had already shared hers. In a speech on November 10, she said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to 2% and that further gradual rate hikes seemed appropriate. She judged underlying inflation to be stuck between 2.5% and 3%. She also named three developments that would lead her to favour moving faster: inflation expectations drifting higher, wage pressures building, or underlying inflation rising. At the same time, she flagged that recent swings in stocks and oil could make consumer spending less durable than expected, one reason she prefers a gradual pace.

Read together, the two speeches point the same way. Paulson is a voter this year, and nothing in either speech suggests she would resist the quarter-point hike in December that markets widely expect, which would lift the target range to 4.00% to 4.25%. Thursday’s message adds that a slower pace should not be mistaken for a softer resolve.

Bitcoin hits lowest since July as Fed hike talk and a Wall Street rout collide
body: The rates message (like this: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) is hitting the whole crypto complex, not just Bitcoin. Ether dropped below $1,800 and sentiment gauges sit at extremes. Spot ETF products traded lower with the underlying, and IBIT and FBTC each fell less than 1% on the day. That leaves crypto equities such as COIN and MSTR, and listed miners, exposed to both falling token prices and a weaker tech tape. Bitcoin is trading as a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge, so equity volatility and Fed pricing remain the main drivers for now.
Bitcoin is trading like a leveraged bet on Fed policy, and Thursday’s mix of hawkish minutes and a stock market rout pushed it to a four-month low.

Bitcoin fell to around $61,600 on Thursday, its lowest level since early July. The move came as a 1,000-point drop in the Dow and fresh talk of tighter Federal Reserve policy pushed investors out of riskier assets. The token was down a little over 2% on the day by early evening in New York, leaving it within reach of the $60,000 mark and roughly half its record high.

The selling tracked Wall Street closely. Bitcoin traded near $63,900 at the US open and slipped to around $62,250 by lunchtime, while the Dow shed more than 1,000 points and the VIX volatility gauge climbed above 28. A short-seller report on AMD added to pressure on tech stocks. Ether dropped below $1,800, and the widely watched Fear and Greed Index sat at 10, deep in extreme fear territory.

Rates are the bigger backdrop. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting, released on Wednesday, showed most officials favour further increases, with some open to a half-point move in December. The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% in October, with two dissenters preferring a quarter-point hike. Since then, a hotter-than-expected October inflation report has met the threshold Governor Christopher Waller had set out for when a 50 basis point increase might be warranted.

Higher rates raise the cost of holding assets that pay no yield, and Bitcoin has been absorbing that message for weeks. It is on course for a seventh straight weekly loss, a run that has taken it from about $87,500 in early October.

Flows offer little support. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw more than $300 million in net outflows on Wednesday, taking November’s total to roughly $2.6 billion, and analysts also point to miners selling into a thinning market.

Traders will watch whether the $60,000 level holds, Thursday’s ETF flow data for any sign that redemptions are slowing, and incoming US data ahead of the Fed’s December meeting. A run of softer numbers could cool hike expectations quickly. Another hot print would likely keep the pressure on.

news.title: Barclays: Back-to-back Fed hikes give the dollar staying power that a jumbo 50bp move wouldn’t
body: The focus for the dollar shifts from how big the December hike will be to how long the hiking continues. That leans toward front-end Treasury yields staying high into the first quarter. It’s a constructive backdrop for the dollar against lower-yielding currencies, although intervention risk near 160 limits the upside in USD/JPY. Gold faces the same headwind it has struggled with all year, as longer-lasting high US rates raise the cost of holding it. Freight and diesel costs are a direct channel from oil to US core inflation, so oil prices now feed straight into Fed pricing.
Barclays says the dollar’s strength comes from how long the Fed keeps hiking, not how big any single move is, and two quarter-point steps do that job better than one jumbo hike.

Barclays says the case for a stronger dollar does not depend on the Federal Reserve delivering a half-point hike in December. In its view, two consecutive quarter-point moves would do more for the currency over time, keeping US rates higher for longer rather than front-loading the tightening in a single step.

The bank’s economists forecast 25 basis point hikes at both the December 8 to 9 and January 26 to 27 meetings. That would lift the federal funds target range from 3.75% to 4.00% now to 4.25% to 4.50% early next year. Barclays does not expect the 50 basis point move that Governor Christopher Waller has argued officials should consider in December. Futures still show a quarter-point December hike as the overwhelming favourite.

The forecast is not new, but Barclays has grown more confident in it. The bank first added a January hike in mid-October, after previously expecting the Fed to stop in December. October’s inflation figures then delivered a run of upside surprises, with headline CPI rising 0.4% on the month against expectations of 0.3%. Barclays says diesel and energy costs are now passing through into a widening set of core categories, with higher freight costs reaching consumer goods. That broadening is the key point. An inflation shock that spreads beyond fuel is harder for the Fed to look through, which argues for sustained tightening rather than one dramatic move.

Barclays has also said that limited prospects for much lower oil prices, solid economic data and hawkish comments from officials all point to more hikes in the near term. That makes the path of crude a direct input into its rate and currency views.

The call puts Barclays in the middle of the tier-one pack. J.P. Morgan, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America expect three consecutive hikes, adding March to the December and January moves, while Goldman Sachs sees a December hike followed by another in March. What unites most of them is the view that the cycle does not end in December, and Barclays sees that as the most supportive part of the story for the dollar.

The dollar index is already near its highest in about 19 months, so the argument is about how durable that strength is rather than whether it exists. A single jumbo hike could be read as the Fed catching up and then stopping. A steady sequence of hikes into 2027 keeps the rate gap with other major economies wider for longer.

news.title: Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven’t quit
body: Gold now trades below most major bank year-end targets, leaving it oversold on fundamentals but without a catalyst to turn it. With the $3,700 handle gone, traders are looking for support in the low $3,600s and high $3,500s, and a clean break would invite more momentum selling. The December 9 Fed decision is the main event risk: a 50 basis point hike or a higher dot plot would extend losses, while any hint the cycle is near its end could spark a sharp short-covering bounce. Miners are still far above record production costs, so margins can absorb further weakness, and supply is unlikely to tighten from producers cutting output.
Gold’s sellers have rates, yields and the dollar on their side, while its buyers are central banks and long-term investors who are patient but too slow to stop the slide.

Gold has slumped to around $3,625 an ounce, about 35% below its record near $5,590 set in late January. Sellers have been in control for most of the year, and the past week has brought some of the heaviest losses yet. The bull case has not disappeared, but it now rests on slower-moving, structural buyers, while the forces pushing prices down are immediate and tied to rates. Here is how the two sides line up.

The biggest weight on gold is the Federal Reserve. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect further hikes, markets see a December move as close to certain, and J.P. Morgan now forecasts hikes in December, January and March. Each step raises the cost of holding a metal that pays no yield. Hawkish signals from the Fed drove gold’s 3% slide this week, its steepest in some time.

The US 10-year Treasury yield is holding above 5%, and the dollar index is near its highest in about 19 months. Together they give investors a competitive return elsewhere and make gold more expensive for buyers outside the US.

Through the Middle East conflict, gold has not behaved as a haven. Escalation pushes oil higher, oil feeds inflation, and inflation feeds expectations of further Fed hikes and higher yields. Renewed US-Iran strikes this month brought no safe-haven buying, with rates outweighing geopolitics.

The outflows are concentrated in the US. North America was the only region with gold ETF outflows in October, and retail bar and coin demand fell about a fifth year on year in the third quarter. The weakness was most visible in Asia’s two biggest consumer markets. Indian bar and coin buying fell about 40%, accounting for most of the global drop, and jewellery demand in both China and India fell by around a fifth as high prices put shoppers off. Silver, down more than 60% from its peak, shows how hard forced selling has hit the wider precious metals complex.

Big banks have been lowering their numbers. Goldman Sachs has cut its outlook twice in less than a month, most recently trimming its end-2027 target to $4,650 from $4,800 after earlier reducing it from $5,400. On the charts, the break below $3,700 removed a closely watched level, and some analysts see the next support areas in the high $3,500s to mid-$3,600s.

The strongest argument for the bulls is official-sector demand. Central banks bought about 321 tonnes in the third quarter, up more than 40% on a year earlier. Goldman Sachs assumes roughly 60 tonnes a month of central bank buying, against about 17 tonnes before 2022, and sees that as the main pillar of its forecast. These purchases tend to show up in data with a lag, so they offer little near-term support for prices.

Global gold ETF holdings reached a record near 4,256 tonnes in October, helped by inflows from European funds. Chinese retail investors have also stayed committed: bar and coin demand in China rose 7% year on year in the third quarter, and its year-to-date total is the highest on record. That suggests the selling is regional rather than a wholesale exit from gold.

Even after the cuts, major bank forecasts are well above the current price. Goldman Sachs sees $4,650 by the end of 2027, Morgan Stanley targets $5,250 for the fourth quarter of 2027, and Deutsche Bank sees a conditional debasement case for 2027 to 2028 if the Fed eventually eases or financial repression returns. The gap between those targets largely reflects different assumptions about rates and official buying.

Gold’s best route back is the end of the hiking cycle. Goldman Sachs’s base case has the Fed cutting from the second half of 2027. Once markets start pricing an end to tightening, the main source of selling pressure would ease.

For now, the sellers. The forces pushing gold lower are fast-moving and tied to rates, while the buyers are patient, price-insensitive and slow to show up in the data. The next key test is the December 9 Fed decision and its projections, which will show how far into 2027 officials expect to keep hiking. Until the rate outlook turns, central bank demand looks more likely to slow the decline than reverse it.

news.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 19 Nov Inflation worries sink stocks
body: Inflation is still the concern. The Philly Fed survey showed manufacturers paying higher prices even as new orders slipped into contraction, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2% target. That leaves the Fed facing persistent price pressure just as some of the activity and labor data are starting to soften. investinglive.com

Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut gave buyers an early reason to step in. The Nasdaq Composite was up more than 2% at its high and finished down 2.25%. Treasuries caught a bid as stocks fell, but the 10-year yield still ended the afternoon above 5%. The dollar firmed, gold and Bitcoin sold off, and the late crude quote held a gain as traders weighed shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. wsj.com

The USD was strongest against the Australian dollar and gained the least against the euro. AUDUSD fell 0.89% to 0.6657 after Australia’s unemployment rate rose to 4.9%. GBPUSD fell 0.49% to 1.3082, while USDJPY was up 0.22% at 159.68 after getting within four pips of 160.00. EURUSD slipped 0.04% to 1.0969. images.investinglive.com

The 2-year yield was up 3.4 basis points at the European close and down 3.4 basis points in late U.S. trading as flight to safety flows sent yields lower. The front end led the reversal as the stock selloff deepened. The 10-year was still above 5%, a level that keeps borrowing costs and stock valuations in focus. images.investinglive.com
The S&P 500 fell for a sixth straight session, with more than 90% of its members lower. Small caps were also down about 2% late in the day. apnews.com

Anthropic priced at $83, opened at $111.50 and reached $115.10 before closing at $97.17, up 17.1% from the offer price. The roughly $81 billion public offering drew strong demand, but the buying failed to carry through to the broader AI trade. AMD fell 7.7% to $489.19 after a Hunterbrook report raised questions about its exposure to U.S. chip export controls on China. images.investinglive.com

The November Philly Fed index fell to 6.3 from 20.9, well below the 20.0 estimate. New orders dropped to −0.4, while prices paid jumped to 58.2 from 43.2, the highest since April. Initial jobless claims edged up to 203K versus 197K expected. The bigger move was in continuing claims, which rose 70K to 1.763 million, suggesting people already out of work may be taking longer to find a job. investinglive.com

Goolsbee described the labor market as stable and consumer demand as solid. He also said tariffs have had a more persistent effect than expected and pointed to the war as another source of inflation. Those remarks kept the focus on price pressure a day after Waller raised the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike in December. Separately, InvestingLive reported, citing CBC, that Canada is seeking an interim U.S. tariff deal by year-end covering sectors including steel, aluminum, autos and lumber. images.investinglive.com

The late U.S. crude quote was $83.99, up $0.73 or 0.88%. December WTI futures officially settled at $83.21, down $0.05. Reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz offered support, while rising U.S. inventories and expectations of a global surplus limited the move. Further disruption would keep energy prices in the Fed’s inflation discussion.

Gold fell 2.69% to $3,624.74, and silver dropped 4.71% to $42.922. The firmer dollar was a headwind, and the late decline in Treasury yields did little to cushion the metals. Copper also fell 1.40% to $5.5890, consistent with caution about industrial demand. Bitcoin slipped 2.20% to $61,592, moving with equities as the early appetite for risk faded.

The next session will show whether buyers can hold a rebound after Thursday’s reversal. The 10-year yield above 5%, Anthropic’s ability to hold its first-day gains and any fresh disruption in Hormuz are the levels and headlines to watch. The Fed’s challenge remains the same. Price pressures are proving persistent while parts of the economy are losing momentum.
